name: Dana Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Fernhill, which is Mrs Okonjo's farm, three thousand free-range laying hens, about thirty hectares of vegetables and a bit of grazing let out to a neighbour's sheep. I run the hen side most days: let them out at seven, check the sensors on the feed and water, collect and grade the eggs, then afternoons I'm in the veg, usually leeks and squash. I'm the one who set up the egg orders on a spreadsheet the AI helps me keep tidy, and I talk to the chatbot about pretty much everything, from red mite to my tax return.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like fixing things, a feeder that jams, an order system that's a mess. What wears me out is the egg prices and the fact that I live on my own, so there's no second wage. I rent a room above the hardware shop and I've got maybe ten days of money put by. On Saturdays I sell microgreens at the market, little trays of pea shoots and radish, which pays for my phone and petrol.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype. Shame, I quite like the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold but it's still handy, and anyone who ignored it completely missed a trick. I'd post a little video about how I use it for the egg orders, because people ask me. Nothing dramatic either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means not much changes and I carry on being the one at Fernhill who's good with the tech. That's useful, but it doesn't pay more. I'd still be living above a hardware shop selling pea shoots on Saturdays to pay for petrol.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools every day. I'd try to grow the microgreens stall a bit, maybe sell to the two cafés in town. I'd ask Mrs Okonjo for a small raise for running the orders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. I like change, and this is no change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would selling to the cafés be worth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they each took ten trays a week, that's maybe sixty a week extra. It's small, but for me that's the difference between ten days of savings and a month by the end of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you stand on all the arguments about AI, politically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere in the middle. I think it's useful and it needs some rules, like anything. I don't trust people who say it'll save the world, and I don't trust people who say it'll end it.

S0.say: It was oversold but still handy, and those who ignored it missed a trick. She'd post a short video showing how she uses it for egg orders.
S0.think: Not much changes and she stays the person who's good with tech, which is useful but doesn't pay more. She'd still be scraping by with a market stall.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools daily. Grows her microgreens stall by selling to two cafés in town for about sixty a week. Asks the farm owner for a small raise for running the orders.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly flat, since she enjoys change.
S0.quote: I'd still be living above a hardware shop selling pea shoots on Saturdays to pay for petrol.
S0.fieldNote: Dana lives alone with about ten days of savings and no second income, which makes her more exposed than she sounds. She's comfortable with tech and already runs a small side business. Her politics are firmly in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that one I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for farms to stop doing the boring bits by hand, and we'd better learn it. I'd be the one at the farmers' market telling people about the sensors and the egg-collecting robots. I'd say there should be some help for people who lose out, but I'd mostly be positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think Mrs Okonjo would bring in automated egg collection and grading, and maybe a weeding robot in the veg. She'd need someone to run it all and I'm the obvious choice. My hands would come out of the egg trays and go onto a tablet, and honestly I wouldn't miss the trays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to research the machines for her and set them up, starting this winter. I'd learn the software properly, using the chatbot and the supplier's videos. I'd use the time I save to grow the microgreens business, maybe a second market on Wednesdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit excited, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your hands would leave the egg trays. What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hens, a bit. When you collect by hand you notice the one who's off colour. I'd have to make sure the cameras did that, or check myself, because I'd hate to miss a sick bird.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at Fernhill you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kev, who does the packing three days a week. He's in his sixties and doesn't want to learn any of it. I'd try to make sure there's still something for him, like the deliveries.

S1.say: It's a chance for farms to stop doing boring work by hand, so we'd better learn it. There should be some help for those who lose out, but she'd be mostly positive.
S1.think: Her boss would bring in automated egg collection and weeding, and Dana would be the obvious person to run it. She wouldn't miss the egg trays.
S1.do: Offers to research and set up the machines this winter. Learns the software through the chatbot and supplier videos. Uses saved time to add a second weekly market for microgreens.
S1.quote: My hands would come out of the egg trays and go onto a tablet, and honestly I wouldn't miss the trays.
S1.fieldNote: Dana sees steady change as a promotion in all but name. Her one worry is animal welfare when she's no longer handling the birds. She thinks of an older colleague and would try to protect his hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Oh. That's not the same at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan from the government, fast, because people will lose jobs before they can do anything. I'd still say the tech is impressive, because it is, but that it's moving faster than people can. I'd be more careful about what I post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this one scares me. If the AI can run the hen house and the robots can do everything else, Mrs Okonjo doesn't need me to set anything up. I'm on my own with ten days of money, and nobody else's wage to fall back on. The microgreens would be done by a robot too, probably cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on everything except rent, food and the van, straight away. I'd try to make as much as I could in the first year, setting up machines for other farms around here while they still need a person. If that dried up, I'd move to wherever there was any work, probably back to my parents' town, which is bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I like change, but not with no floor under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say if you turned up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say I told you farming doesn't pay. My mum would make up the bed. I'd let him say it, because I'd need the bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're someone who likes change. Why does this one feel different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like change when I can get ahead of it. Two years isn't enough to get ahead of anything. Being early only helps if there's somewhere to land.

S2.say: The government needs a plan fast because people will lose jobs before they can act. The tech is impressive but moving faster than people can.
S2.think: The farm wouldn't need her to set anything up if AI can run it. Living alone with ten days of savings and no other wage, she'd have nothing to fall back on.
S2.do: Cuts spending to rent, food and the van immediately. Sells machine setup work to local farms in the first year while it's still needed. Moves back to her parents' larger town if that work dries up.
S2.feel: Alarmed, because she likes change but not without a safety net.
S2.quote: I'm on my own with ten days of money, and nobody else's wage to fall back on.
S2.fieldNote: This scenario flips Dana from enthusiast to alarmed, and the reason is clear: she's single with almost no savings. She explains that being early only helps if there's somewhere to land. Her parents are her real backup, despite her father's teasing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's different again. That's enough to get ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the next few years are the time to get ready, and I'd tell other farmers to start learning now. I'd probably run a little workshop at the market on using the AI tools, free, because people would want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think five years is enough for me to get a couple of years of setup work and save something. It still ends with the farm not needing me, but I'd have money and contacts by then. Five years is long enough for me to be the person who helped the robots arrive, and get paid for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start doing setup work for other farms in the evenings this year, charging a fair rate. I'd put most of it away, aiming for three months of savings by the end of year two. In year three I'd look at a proper course, maybe in robotics or agricultural tech, and think about a job with a supplier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's still a big change, but I'd feel I had hold of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a fair rate be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe thirty an hour to start, since I'm not certified. Older farmers would pay that to have someone sit with them and set up the egg sensors properly. Ten hours a month would double what the microgreens bring in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They give me a floor. In two years I'm grabbing work and running home. In five I can build savings and a reputation, and then pick where to go next.

S3.say: The next few years are the time to get ready, and farmers should start learning now. She'd run a free market workshop on using AI tools.
S3.think: Five years gives her a couple of years of paid setup work, savings and contacts before the farm stops needing her. She'd be paid to help the robots arrive.
S3.do: Starts evening setup work for other farms this year at around thirty an hour. Saves most of it, aiming for three months of savings by the end of year two. Takes a robotics or agricultural tech course in year three.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but feeling she has hold of it.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough for me to be the person who helped the robots arrive, and get paid for it.
S3.fieldNote: For Dana, the extra time is the difference between scrambling and building a floor. She has clear numbers and a timeline. She'd teach others for free, which fits her practical, sociable streak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That sounds like an opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this could be good for farming if we plan it, and that young people should be learning robotics in agricultural college now. I'd say there should be support for older workers. I'd be positive, but I'd say it carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is enough to change career properly and come out the other side. I'd want to work for a company that makes or installs farm robots, and maybe end up running my own small business doing it. I'd swap the hen house for the van that drives round fixing everybody's hen houses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the evening setup work and save, same as the five-year plan. By year two I'd do a part-time course in agricultural technology. By year four or five I'd apply to a supplier, and if I liked it, start my own service business later on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd actually look forward to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you need to move for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a few years, to where the suppliers are. I wouldn't mind, I'm on my own and I rent a room. The thing that makes me scared in the two-year picture makes me free in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who won't change. Kev, Mrs Okonjo even. I'd worry about the ones who wait until it's too late. I can't make anyone learn.

S4.say: This could be good for farming if it's planned, and young people should learn robotics now. There should be support for older workers.
S4.think: Ten years is enough to change careers properly, perhaps installing farm robots and later running her own service business.
S4.do: Starts evening setup work and saves. Takes a part-time agricultural technology course by year two. Applies to a robot supplier by year four or five, possibly moving, and later starts her own service business.
S4.feel: Calm and looking forward to it, though she worries about people who won't adapt.
S4.quote: The thing that makes me scared in the two-year picture makes me free in this one.
S4.fieldNote: Dana's single life is a weakness with two years' notice and a freedom with ten, and she says this herself. She sees herself driving a repair van rather than working inside a farm. Her worry shifts entirely to others who won't change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm on my own with ten days of money, and being early is no use when there's nowhere to land. What would help is a basic wage for a year while people switch, and cheap short courses in farm tech, run locally, not in the city.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but someone has to make sure the robots notice when a hen's sick. I'd want that in the rules.

headlineQuote: I'd swap the hen house for the van that drives round fixing everybody's hen houses.
portrait: Dana Haddad is a 27-year-old who runs the laying hen side of a poultry and vegetable farm and sells microgreens at the Saturday market. She lives alone in a rented room with about ten days of savings, uses AI tools every day and enjoys fixing things. Pragmatic and in the middle politically, she's calm at a plateau and excited about steady change. AGI in two years alarms her because she has no second income or safety net. With five or ten years she plans paid setup work for local farms, a technology course and a career installing farm robots, and sees being single as a freedom.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she lives alone with ten days of savings and would have nowhere to land.
whatWouldHelp: A basic wage for a year while people switch, and cheap, local short courses in farm technology.
